scene.title: REST vs GraphQL: API Design Tradeoffs
scene.subtitle: Choosing a query model as an API surface grows

answer.headline: REST wins on simplicity, caching, and tooling maturity; GraphQL wins when clients need flexible, precisely-shaped data from a large, evolving schema.
body: REST organizes an API around resources and HTTP verbs: a client fetches or mutates a URL that represents one entity or collection at a time. This maps cleanly onto HTTP caching, is easy to reason about, and every HTTP client, proxy, and monitoring tool already understands it. The cost shows up as the API grows: a mobile screen that needs data from four resources either makes four round trips or waits for a bespoke aggregation endpoint, and a single resource often ships more fields than any one client actually uses.

GraphQL flips the contract: the client sends a query describing exactly the fields and nested relations it wants, and the server resolves that shape in one round trip. This removes over-fetching and under-fetching almost entirely, and a single schema can serve a web app, a mobile app, and a partner integration without three sets of endpoints. The cost moves to the server: naive resolvers can trigger the N+1 query problem, arbitrary nesting needs depth and complexity limits, and HTTP-level caching no longer works out of the box because every request is a POST to the same URL.

Versioning also diverges. REST APIs typically version whole endpoints (v1, v2) or negotiate via headers, which is coarse but predictable. GraphQL favors additive evolution: new fields are added and old ones are deprecated in place, so a single schema version can serve old and new clients simultaneously, at the cost of needing schema governance to stop it from sprawling.

Tooling maturity still favors REST for anything that leans on generic HTTP infrastructure: CDNs, simple rate limiters, and off-the-shelf API gateways. GraphQL's tooling has caught up for introspection, typed client generation, and query cost analysis, but it usually means adopting a GraphQL-aware layer rather than reusing whatever HTTP tooling is already on hand.

In practice, teams with a small number of well-known clients and a resource model that maps naturally onto CRUD tend to be happier with REST. Teams serving several very different client types against a wide, fast-changing data graph tend to be happier with GraphQL, provided they invest in resolver-level caching and query complexity limits from day one.
caveats: Hybrid approaches (REST with sparse fieldsets, or GraphQL over a thin REST layer) are common in practice and blur this comparison.
GraphQL's caching gap can be closed with persisted queries and edge caching, but it takes deliberate setup that REST gets for free.
Team familiarity with either paradigm often outweighs the technical tradeoffs discussed here.

modules.headline: A quick way to pick a direction

items.label: Count client shapes
items.detail: One or two well-known clients with similar needs usually points toward REST's simplicity.

items.label: Check data graph width
items.detail: A large graph of related entities that different clients slice differently favors GraphQL's flexible queries.

items.label: Weigh caching needs
items.detail: If CDN-level caching of responses is load-bearing for performance, REST keeps that for free.

items.label: Assess team readiness
items.detail: GraphQL needs someone accountable for resolver performance and query complexity limits from day one.

modules.headline: A GraphQL query asking for exactly what it needs
Pick the model that matches your client diversity
modules.body: Neither model is strictly better: REST optimizes for a small, stable set of clients and free HTTP infrastructure, while GraphQL optimizes for many client shapes pulling from one evolving graph. Most teams that regret their choice picked GraphQL for a single, simple client, or picked REST for a product that grew five very different frontends. Match the model to how many different ways your data actually gets sliced, not to which one is trending.
